title: Cambridge International AS & A Level Business (9609)

officialDocument.title: Cambridge International AS & A Level Business 9609 syllabus for 2026, 2027 and 2028 (version 2, published December 2025)
officialDocument.publisher: Cambridge University Press & Assessment (Cambridge International Education)

sourceNote: Topic and sub-topic headings (1.1 Enterprise ... 10.4.2 The use of accounting data and ratio analysis in strategic decision-making) are transcribed with their printed numbers. The syllabus lists bullets without numbers: objective codes (1.1.1.1 ...) are ours, and the bullets are paraphrased in our own words. The two sections (AS and A) are ours, following the syllabus's own split of AS Level topics 1.1-5.5 and A Level topics 6.1-10.4. No syllabus text is reproduced.
notes: Source (read 2026-10-10): the official PDF 'Cambridge International AS & A Level Business 9609 syllabus for 2026, 2027 and 2028', version 2 (published December 2025, no significant changes affecting teaching), read through a pdftotext rendering. Exams in the June and November series (March for India). Check headings and the notes against the PDF.

Routes as printed: AS Level only (Papers 1 and 2 in one series; grades a-e); A Level staged over two years (AS in year 1, carried forward, then Papers 3 and 4); A Level in one series (all four papers; grades A*-E). Route A here covers both A Level routes.

Weightings: Paper 1 40% of AS and 20% of A Level; Paper 2 60% and 30%; Paper 3 30% of A Level; Paper 4 20% of A Level. weightingPercent records the A Level share; the AS shares are in each paper's description. Assessment objectives by qualification: AS AO1 30%, AO2 30%, AO3 20%, AO4 20%; A Level 25% each. By component: Paper 1 AO1 35, AO2 30, AO3 20, AO4 15; Paper 2 30, 30, 20, 20; Paper 3 20, 27, 23, 30; Paper 4 10, 35, 15, 40.

Papers: Paper 1 (1 hour 15 minutes, 40 marks): Section A four compulsory questions of 5 marks (the first three have two parts), Section B two essay questions of 20 marks, answer one (two parts, the second showing evaluation). Paper 2 (1 hour 30 minutes, 60 marks): two compulsory data response questions of 30 marks, six parts each, the last part evaluation. Paper 3 (1 hour 45 minutes, 60 marks): five compulsory questions on a case study (insert): Q1 and Q2 8 marks, Q3 and Q4 16 marks (three and two parts), Q5 12 marks; the last part of Q3 and Q4 and Q5 show evaluation. Paper 4 (1 hour 15 minutes, 40 marks): two compulsory essay questions of 20 marks on a case study, both showing evaluation. Papers 1 and 2 test the AS content (topics 1.1-5.5); Papers 3 and 4 the A Level content (6.1-10.4) with AS content assumed. The division of each essay into parts of 8 and 12 marks is our convention (the syllabus gives only totals).

Topics 1.1-5.5 are AS content; topics 6.1-10.4 are A Level only. Several ZIMSEC topics that are Form 5 or Form 6 content fall in the A Level part for Cambridge (political and legal environment, government and the economy, business strategy, organisational structure, communication, leadership, elasticity, forecasting, location and scale, quality, ERP, lean production, critical path analysis, the statements, ratio analysis and investment appraisal): write them once at A Level depth.

Formulae: the Appendix (Ratios to support analysis of published accounts) gives the only accepted ratio formulae: gross profit margin, operating (profit from operations) margin, ROCE with capital employed = issued shares + reserves + non-current liabilities, current ratio, acid test, trade receivables and payables turnover in days (credit sales and credit purchases x 365), rate of inventory turnover (cost of sales over average inventory), gearing (non-current liabilities over capital employed), price/earnings, dividend yield and dividend cover. Ratios are not printed in question papers.

Accounting Rate of Return: the syllabus prints 'ARR = (average profit/average investment) x 100' without saying how the average investment is found. Past mark schemes are commonly read as average annual profit over the initial investment; the kit therefore requires every item to state the formula and the basis used. A reviewer must confirm the intended basis with the Cambridge teacher guide (not in the repository).
Not examined (stated in the syllabus): drawing up a full set of accounts (candidates calculate ratios and use them); the straight-line method only for depreciation. No other exclusions are printed.

The syllabus runs from 2026 to 2028 inclusive, so effectiveFrom 2026-01-01 and effectiveTo 2028-12-31. Candidates from 2029 will follow a later syllabus (not in the repository); check the Cambridge website for it and add a new version file.
overview: Cambridge International AS & A Level Business (9609) focuses on how decisions are made in businesses, with six key concepts: change, context, decision-making, enterprise, innovation and strategy. The AS Level content covers business and its environment (enterprise, structure, size, objectives, stakeholders), human resource management and motivation, marketing (the nature of marketing, market research and the marketing mix), operations management (the transformational process, inventory, capacity) and finance and accounting (finance, sources, cash flow, costs, break-even, budgets). The A Level content adds the external environment and business strategy, organisational structure, communication, leadership and HRM strategy, marketing analysis and strategy, location, scale, quality and operations strategy, and finance and accounting (financial statements, ratio analysis, investment appraisal and accounting strategy).
assessmentOverview: AS Level candidates take Paper 1 Business Concepts 1 (1 hour 15 minutes, 40 marks) and Paper 2 Business Concepts 2 (1 hour 30 minutes, 60 marks). A Level candidates also take Paper 3 Business Decision-Making (1 hour 45 minutes, 60 marks, a case study) and Paper 4 Business Strategy (1 hour 15 minutes, 40 marks, a case study), in the same series or a later one, carrying forward their AS result.

components.name: Paper 1: Business Concepts 1
components.description: Section A: four short-answer questions of five marks (the first three have two parts). Section B: one essay from a choice of two (20 marks, two parts). AS Level content (topics 1.1-5.5). 40% of AS Level, 20% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 2: Business Concepts 2
components.description: Two compulsory data response questions of 30 marks, six parts each, the last part showing evaluation. AS Level content (topics 1.1-5.5). 60% of AS Level, 30% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 3: Business Decision-Making
components.description: Five compulsory questions based on a case study (insert): questions 1 and 2 of 8 marks, questions 3 and 4 of 16 marks (three and two parts) and question 5 of 12 marks. A Level content (topics 6.1-10.4), AS Level assumed. 30% of A Level.

components.name: Paper 4: Business Strategy
components.description: Two compulsory essay questions of 20 marks each based on a case study, both showing evaluation. A Level content (topics 6.1-10.4), AS Level assumed. 20% of A Level.

routes.name: AS Level
routes.description: Papers 1 and 2 (grades a-e). Also the first year of the staged A Level route.

routes.name: A Level
routes.description: All four papers, in one series or staged (AS Level carried forward, then Papers 3 and 4) (grades A*-E).

topics.name: AS Level subject content (topics 1.1-5.5)
topics.description: Assessed by Papers 1 and 2 and assumed knowledge for Papers 3 and 4. Content areas: 1 Business and its environment, 2 Human resource management, 3 Marketing, 4 Operations management, 5 Finance and accounting.

objectives.text: Explain the purpose of business activity, the factors of production, adding value, scarcity, choice and opportunity cost.
Explain the dynamic business environment, why businesses succeed or fail, and the differences between local, national, international and multinational businesses.

children.name: The role of entrepreneurs and intrapreneurs

objectives.text: Assess the qualities and roles of entrepreneurs and intrapreneurs, barriers to entrepreneurship, risk and uncertainty and the role of enterprise in a country's development.
Explain the meaning, purpose, key elements, benefits and limitations of business plans.
Distinguish the primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary sectors and the public and private sectors, and explain the reasons for and consequences of changes in their relative importance.
Describe sole traders, partnerships, private and public limited companies, franchises, co-operatives, joint ventures and social enterprises and judge which suits a business.
Explain unlimited and limited liability and the advantages and disadvantages of changing from one type of ownership to another.
Judge the appropriateness of different methods of measuring the size of a business.
Assess the advantages and disadvantages of being small, the strengths and weaknesses of family businesses, and the importance and role of small businesses in the economy and in some industries.
Explain why and how a business grows internally and the types of external growth: horizontal, vertical (backward and forward) and conglomerate mergers, friendly mergers and hostile takeovers.
Assess the impact of mergers and takeovers on stakeholders, why they may or may not achieve their objectives, and the role of joint ventures and strategic alliances.

children.name: Business objectives in the private sector and public sector

objectives.text: Explain the objectives of private-sector, public-sector and social-enterprise organisations, the importance of objectives, corporate social responsibility and the triple bottom line.
Explain the relationship between mission statement, aims, objectives, strategy and tactics.
Explain the stages of decision-making, how objectives change, the translation of objectives into targets and budgets and SMART objectives.
Assess the need to communicate objectives and the way ethics influence objectives and activities.
Distinguish internal from external stakeholders and explain their roles, rights and responsibilities.

children.name: The relative importance and influence of stakeholders on business activities
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 1.5.1.

objectives.text: Assess the impact of decisions on stakeholders and of stakeholder aims on decisions, accountability to stakeholders and conflict between stakeholders' aims.

children.name: Human resource management (2 Human resource management)
Purpose and roles of HRM
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 2.1.2.

objectives.text: Explain the role of HRM in meeting organisational objectives.
Explain the reasons for and role of a workforce plan and measure labour turnover.
Assess the implications of high and low labour turnover.
Explain the recruitment process (job descriptions, person specifications, methods, internal and external recruitment), selection methods and employment contracts.
Distinguish redundancy (voluntary and involuntary) from dismissal (fair and unfair).
Explain the relationship between HRM, morale and welfare, including work-life balance, and the impact of diversity and equality on a business.
Distinguish induction, on-the-job and off-the-job training and assess the impact of training and development, including for intrapreneurship, multi-skilling and flexibility.
Explain how cooperation between management and workforce benefits both, and the impact of trade unions and collective bargaining on employers and employees.

children.name: Motivation as a tool of management and leadership
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 2.2.2.

objectives.text: Explain the need to motivate employees to achieve business objectives.
Explain human need and how needs may or may not be satisfied at work.
Explain the content theories of Taylor, Mayo, Maslow, Herzberg and McClelland and the process theory of Vroom.

children.name: Motivation methods in practice: financial motivators, non-financial motivators

objectives.text: Apply the theories to practical situations and assess payment methods (time based, salary, piece rates, commission, bonuses, profit sharing, performance-related pay, fringe benefits).
Assess non-financial motivators (training, promotion, status, job re-design, team working, empowerment, participation, job enrichment) and ways of employee participation.
Explain the functions of managers (planning, organising, directing, controlling), the roles of managers (Fayol, Mintzberg) and their contribution to performance.
Distinguish autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire and paternalistic styles and McGregor's Theory X and Theory Y managers.

children.name: The role of marketing and its relationship with other business activities

objectives.text: Explain marketing objectives and their link to corporate objectives (with customer relationship marketing, 3.1.7).
Explain the factors influencing demand and supply and the interactions between demand, supply and price.
Explain how markets differ, product against customer orientation, the measurement of market share and growth, and the implications of changes in them.

children.name: Consumer and industrial marketing
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 3.1.3.

objectives.text: Classify products and explain how marketing differs for consumer (B2C) and industrial (B2B) products.

children.name: Mass marketing and niche marketing
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 3.1.6.

objectives.text: Explain the features, advantages and disadvantages of mass and niche marketing.
Explain geographic, demographic and psychographic segmentation and its advantages and disadvantages.

children.name: Customer relationship marketing (CRM)
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 3.1.1.

objectives.text: Explain the aims, costs and benefits of customer relationship marketing.

children.name: The purposes of market research
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 3.2.2.

objectives.text: Explain how research identifies the features of a market and customers' characteristics, wants and needs.
Distinguish primary from secondary research and assess the usefulness of data from each.

children.name: Sampling
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 3.2.2.

objectives.text: Explain the need for and limitations of sampling.
Judge the reliability of data, analyse quantitative and qualitative data and interpret tables, charts and graphs.

children.name: The elements of the marketing mix (the 4Ps)
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 3.3.2.

objectives.text: Identify the 4Ps: product, price, promotion and place (distribution channels).
Distinguish goods from services and tangible from intangible attributes; explain the importance of product development, product differentiation and the unique selling point.
Use the product life cycle and extension strategies and the Boston Matrix and assess their impact on marketing decisions.
Assess the objectives and usefulness of competitive, penetration, skimming, price discrimination, dynamic, cost-based and psychological pricing.
Assess advertising, sales promotion, direct promotion and developments in digital promotion, and the roles of packaging and branding in promotion.
Assess the objectives and usefulness of different channels of distribution, digital and physical.

children.name: The nature of operations (4 Operations management)

objectives.text: Explain the use of the factors of production, the stages from inputs to outputs and the contribution of operations to added value.
Explain the importance of efficiency, effectiveness, productivity and sustainability, measure labour productivity and assess the impact of measures to improve sustainability.

children.name: Capital intensive and labour intensive operations
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 4.1.4.

objectives.text: Assess the benefits and limitations of capital-intensive and labour-intensive operations.

children.name: Operations methods: job, batch, flow, mass customisation

objectives.text: Distinguish job, batch, flow and mass customisation methods, assess their advantages and disadvantages and the problems of changing from one to another.
Explain the purpose, costs and benefits of inventory, buffer inventory, re-order level, lead time, simple inventory control charts and the importance of supply chain management.
Explain the purpose of JIT and JIC and the impact of adopting JIT on a business.

children.name: Significance and measurement of capacity utilisation

objectives.text: Measure capacity utilisation, assess the impact of operating under or over capacity and explain methods of improving utilisation.

children.name: Outsourcing
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 4.3.1.

objectives.text: Assess the impact of outsourcing on a business.
Explain why businesses need finance to start up, grow and survive, short and long term needs, the difference between cash and profit, and failure through lack of finance.
Explain the meaning and importance of working capital, the management of trade receivables and payables, and the difference between capital and revenue expenditure.

children.name: Business ownership and sources of finance
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 5.2.4.

objectives.text: Explain the relationship between the form of ownership and the sources of finance available.

children.name: Internal and external sources of finance

objectives.text: Assess internal sources (owner's investment, retained earnings, sale of assets, sale and leaseback, working capital).

Assess external sources (share capital, debentures, new partners, venture capital, overdrafts, leasing, hire purchase, loans, mortgages, debt factoring, trade credit, micro-finance, crowd funding, grants).

children.name: Factors affecting the sources of finance
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 5.2.4.

objectives.text: Explain the influence of cost, flexibility, control, use of funds and existing debt on the choice of finance.
Judge the appropriateness of each possible source of finance in a given situation.
Explain the meaning and purpose of cash flow forecasts, interpret and amend simple forecasts (opening and closing balances) and assess methods of improving cash flow.
Explain the need for accurate cost information and classify fixed, variable, direct and indirect costs.
Distinguish full from contribution costing, their uses and limitations, contribution from profit, and when each is used.

children.name: Uses of cost information
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 5.4.2.

objectives.text: Use average, marginal and total cost in decisions, in pricing and to monitor performance, and use contribution costing in special order decisions.
Calculate and interpret break-even output, contribution, margin of safety and profit in numeric and graphic form, and assess the uses and limitations of break-even analysis.

children.name: The meaning and purpose of budgets

objectives.text: Explain budgets and the measurement of performance, benefits and drawbacks, incremental, flexible and zero budgeting, and the uses of budgets in allocating resources and controlling a business.

children.name: Variances
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 5.5.1.

objectives.text: Calculate and interpret adverse and favourable variances.

topics.name: A Level subject content (topics 6.1-10.4)
topics.description: A Level only: assessed by Papers 3 and 4 (the AS Level content is assumed knowledge). Content areas: 6 Business and its environment, 7 Human resource management, 8 Marketing, 9 Operations management, 10 Finance and accounting.

children.name: External influences on business activity (6 Business and its environment)

objectives.text: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of privatisation and nationalisation in a given situation.

Explain how a government may use the law to control employment practices, conditions of work, wages, marketing behaviour, competition, location and particular goods, and the impact of political and legal change.

Explain how government helps or constrains business, deals with market failure, and the macroeconomic objectives and policies (monetary, fiscal, supply-side, exchange rate) and their impact on business.
Assess corporate social responsibility issues, the needs of the community and pressure groups, and the impact of social and demographic change (see also 6.1.7).
Assess the impact of technological change on business and decisions (competitors and suppliers, 6.1.5).

children.name: Competitors and suppliers
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 6.1.4.

objectives.text: Assess the impact of competitors and suppliers on business and decisions.

Assess the importance of international trading links and trade agreements, the role of technology in trade, and the advantages and disadvantages of multinationals and their relationships with governments.

children.name: Environmental
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 6.1.3.

objectives.text: Explain how physical environmental issues influence behaviour, environmental audits and the growing importance of sustainability.
Apply SWOT, PEST, Porter's five forces, blue ocean strategy, scenario planning, the core competence framework, the Ansoff matrix, force field analysis and decision trees to develop strategy.
Explain the meaning and purpose of strategy and strategic management (analysis, choice, implementation), corporate planning, corporate culture and transformational leadership.
Assess the management and control of strategic change and contingency planning and crisis management.

children.name: The relationship between business objectives and organisational structure

objectives.text: Explain the purpose and attributes of an organisational structure and its features: hierarchy, chain of command, span of control, responsibility and authority.

children.name: Types of structure: functional, hierarchical (flat and narrow), matrix

objectives.text: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of each type, structuring by product, function or area, and why and how structures change (growth, delayering).
Explain the relationship between delegation and accountability and the impact of delegation (with 7.1.4).

children.name: Control, authority and trust
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 7.1.3.

objectives.text: Explain span of control against levels of hierarchy, authority against responsibility, and the conflict between control and trust.

children.name: Centralisation and decentralisation
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 7.1.6.

objectives.text: Assess the impact of centralisation and decentralisation on a business.
Distinguish line from staff functions and explain the conflicts between them.

children.name: Purposes of communication
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 7.2.2.

objectives.text: Identify situations in which communication is essential.
Assess the strengths and weaknesses of spoken, written, electronic and visual methods of communication.
Explain one- and two-way and vertical and horizontal communication and the problems of each channel (with barriers and the role of management, 7.2.4 and 7.2.5).

children.name: Barriers to communication
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 7.2.3.

objectives.text: Explain barriers to communication and how to overcome them.

children.name: The role of management in facilitating communication
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 7.2.3.

objectives.text: Assess informal communication, the effect of communication on efficiency and ways of improving communication in a situation.
Explain the purpose of leadership, leadership roles (directors, managers, supervisors, worker representatives) and the qualities of a good leader.
Assess trait, behavioural, contingency, power and influence, and transformational theories of leadership (with Goleman's emotional intelligence, 7.3.3).

children.name: Emotional intelligence / emotional quotient (EQ)
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 7.3.2.

objectives.text: Explain Goleman's four competencies: self-awareness, social awareness, self-management and social skills.

Distinguish hard from soft HRM and assess flexible working contracts (temporary, zero hours, part-time, annualised hours, flexi-time, home working, shift working, job sharing, compressed hours, the gig economy).
Assess the measurement, causes and consequences of poor employee performance, strategies for improvement, management by objectives and the changing role of IT and AI in HRM.
Calculate and interpret price, income and promotional elasticity of demand and assess their impact on decisions and limitations.
Explain the process of product development, sources of new ideas and the importance of R&D.
Explain the need to forecast sales, calculate and use the four-period centred moving average, and assess qualitative forecasting and the impact on decisions.
Explain the contents of a marketing plan and its benefits and limitations (with approaches to strategy and the role of IT and AI, 8.2.2).

children.name: Approaches to marketing strategy
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 8.2.1.

objectives.text: Assess the need for a coordinated marketing strategy consistent with the business, product and market and the changing role of IT and AI in marketing.
Assess the implications of globalisation, identification, selection and entry into international markets, pan-global marketing against local differences and the method of entry.
Explain the factors that determine location and relocation, local, national and international decisions, offshoring and reshoring and the impact of globalisation (scale of operations, 9.1.2).

children.name: Scale of operations
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 9.1.1.

objectives.text: Explain the factors that influence the scale of a business, internal and external economies and diseconomies of scale and their links to unit costs.
Explain quality as meeting customer expectations and the impact of quality control, quality assurance and total quality management (with benchmarking, 9.2.2).

children.name: Benchmarking
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 9.2.1.

objectives.text: Explain the importance of benchmarking in quality management.
Explain the influence of human, marketing and finance resources on operations decisions and the changing role of IT and AI (with flexibility and innovation, 9.3.2).

children.name: Flexibility and innovation
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 9.3.1.

objectives.text: Explain the need for flexibility in volume, delivery time and specification and process innovation.
Explain the main features of ERP and how it improves efficiency in inventory control, costing, capacity utilisation, response to change, workforce flexibility and management information.

Explain the aims of lean production, the strategies used (kaizen, quality circles, simultaneous engineering, cell production, JIT, waste management) and their limitations and links to other functions.
Draw and use network diagrams for critical path analysis: minimum duration, critical path, total and free float, use in project management, benefits and limitations.
Explain the purpose and contents of the statement of profit or loss, amend it and assess the impact of a given change.
Explain the purpose and contents of the statement of financial position, amend it and explain the relationships with the statement of profit or loss.

children.name: Inventory valuation
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 10.1.4.

objectives.text: Explain the difficulties of valuing inventory and the net realisable value method.
Explain the role of depreciation in the accounts and its impact (straight-line method only) on the statements.
Calculate and interpret the current ratio and acid test ratio and assess methods of improving liquidity.
Calculate and interpret return on capital employed, gross profit margin and profit margin and assess methods of improving profitability.
Calculate and interpret rate of inventory turnover, trade receivables turnover (days) and trade payables turnover (days) and assess methods of improving efficiency.

children.name: Gearing ratio
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 10.2.5.

objectives.text: Calculate and interpret the gearing ratio and assess methods of improving gearing.
Calculate and interpret dividend yield, dividend cover and the price/earnings ratio and assess methods of improving investor return.

children.name: The concept of investment appraisal
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 10.3.2.

objectives.text: Explain the need for investment appraisal.

children.name: Basic methods: payback, accounting rate of return (ARR)

objectives.text: Calculate and interpret payback and the accounting rate of return.

children.name: Discounted cash flow method: net present value (NPV)

objectives.text: Calculate and interpret net present value (with investment decisions, 10.3.4).

children.name: Investment appraisal decisions
children.description: Taught in the lesson attached to 10.3.3.

objectives.text: Assess quantitative results and qualitative factors in investment decisions and compare the methods and their limitations.

children.name: The use of accounting data to enable strategic decision-making

objectives.text: Explain how financial statements are used to develop strategies and the contents of an annual report and their usefulness to the business and other stakeholders.

children.name: The use of accounting data and ratio analysis in strategic decision-making

objectives.text: Assess performance over time and against competitors, the impact of debt or equity, dividend, growth and other strategies on ratio results, and the limitations of published accounts and ratio analysis.
